summary:
SANCHAR: Astronaut Health System
SANCHAR is a single-page web app that works as a personal health companion for an astronaut on a 210-day journey to Mars. It brings together vitals monitoring (heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, hydration, radiation dose), an interactive body map showing how microgravity affects muscles, bones and organs, and a mental wellbeing toolkit with breathing exercises, mood tracking, thought reframing and Earth soundscapes. It also includes drills for solar storms, fires and pressure loss, a Health Analysis Lab with a score and bone and muscle forecast, travel tools such as a Mars sol clock and life support calculator, and an AI-style guide named Lyka.
It addresses NASA's five human-spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity, and closed environments. On a Mars mission, rescue is impossible and messages are delayed, so astronauts must manage their own health. SANCHAR makes that practical through daily habits, quick-reference guidance, and gamified quests, quizzes and a Rocket Run game that keep people engaged.
This matters because long-duration missions depend on crew autonomy. The same ideas of self-monitoring, preventive routines and mental resilience also apply to remote and isolated communities on Earth.
details:
What it does

SANCHAR is a health companion for one astronaut on a long trip to Mars. We imagined how it would feel to be 210 days from home, with help minutes away by message and months away by ship, and we built the app we'd want in that situation.

You open it and see your vitals, a mission clock and a daily brief from Lyka, a friendly guide who answers questions. From there you can explore a body map showing what microgravity does to your bones and muscles, try a breathing exercise after a rough day, log your mood, or rehearse what to do in a solar storm or a fire. There's also a travel kit with a Mars sol clock and a life support calculator, and a small arcade game, Rocket Run, because even astronauts need something fun. Everything saves in the browser, so it keeps working offline.

Why it matters

On a Mars mission the crew can't count on rescue, so looking after your own health becomes part of the job. SANCHAR helps by turning that into small daily habits, early warnings and practised emergency responses, covering the five hazards NASA highlights: radiation, isolation, distance, gravity and closed environments. We also hope the same ideas help people in remote places on Earth who have to manage without quick access to care.

How we built it

It's one HTML file in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks and no server. Canvas and SVG draw the body map, charts and game, Web Audio plays the soundscapes, and Google Fonts gives it its look. It needs no special hardware, just a browser.

What makes it creative

We wanted it to feel like a companion, not a spreadsheet. Quests, XP, a game and a named guide make healthy routines feel rewarding, and the body map lets you see what space does to you. We also put physical health, mental health and emergencies in one calm place, because they affect each other.

What we thought about

We kept coming back to four things: the crew's independence, mental health as much as physical, an interface that stays simple under stress and on a small screen, and honesty about limits. The data is sample data and the score uses a simple model, so SANCHAR is a prototype, not a medical tool.
dataRefs: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
